rows.stem: Direction ratios of lines \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) respectively are \(<1, 0, 0>\) and \(<0, -1, 0>\). The direction ratios of the line perpendicular to both \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are :
rows.solution: A line perpendicular to two given lines has direction ratios given by the cross product of their direction ratios. Here \(\langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle \times \langle 0, -1, 0 \rangle = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = (0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot (-1))\hat{i} - (1 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 0)\hat{j} + (1 \cdot (-1) - 0 \cdot 0)\hat{k} = -\hat{k}\). So the required direction ratios are \(\langle 0, 0, -1 \rangle\). This is geometrically obvious as well: the two given lines are along the x-axis and the y-axis, so a line perpendicular to both is along the z-axis. Checking the dot products, \(\langle 0, 0, -1 \rangle \cdot \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle = 0\) and \(\langle 0, 0, -1 \rangle \cdot \langle 0, -1, 0 \rangle = 0\). Hence the answer is option (B) \(\langle 0, 0, -1 \rangle\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.solution: The inverse cosine is defined only when its argument lies in \([-1, 1]\), so we need \(-1 \le 4x + 1 \le 1\). Subtracting 1 throughout gives \(-2 \le 4x \le 0\), and dividing by 4 gives \(-\dfrac{1}{2} \le x \le 0\). Hence the domain is \(\left[-\dfrac{1}{2}, 0\right]\), which is option (D) \(\left[-\dfrac{1}{2}, 0\right]\).

rows.stem: If a matrix X is such that \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} X = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), then the order of matrix X is :
rows.solution: Use the rule that an \(m \times n\) matrix times an \(n \times p\) matrix gives an \(m \times p\) matrix. The left factor \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) has order \(1 \times 2\) and the product \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) has order \(1 \times 3\). If X has order \(m \times n\), then for \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}X\) to be defined we need \(m = 2\), and the product then has order \(1 \times n\). Matching \(1 \times n\) against \(1 \times 3\) gives \(n = 3\). So the order of the matrix X is \(2 \times 3\), which is option (B) \(2 \times 3\).

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem: If \(A(\text{adj } A) = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), then the value of \(|2A|\) is :
rows.solution: For a square matrix A of order n, \(A(\text{adj } A) = |A|I\). The given product is 3 times the identity matrix of order 3, so \(|A| = 3\). Now use \(|kA| = k^{n}|A|\) for a matrix of order n; with \(k = 2\) and \(n = 3\) this gives \(|2A| = 2^3 |A| = 8 \times 3 = 24\). (The common slip is to write \(|2A| = 2|A| = 6\), which ignores that all three rows are scaled.) Hence the value is 24, which is option (D) \(24\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.solution: Rewrite the relation so that x is the subject: \(2\cos^{-1} x = y\) gives \(\cos^{-1} x = \dfrac{y}{2}\) and hence \(x = \cos\dfrac{y}{2}\). Differentiating with respect to y, \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{y}{2}\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{dx/dy} = \dfrac{-2}{\sin\frac{y}{2}} = -2\operatorname{cosec}\dfrac{y}{2}\). (The choice \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{y}{2}\) is \(\dfrac{dx}{dy}\), not \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).) Hence the derivative is \(-2\operatorname{cosec}\dfrac{y}{2}\), which is option (D) \(-2\operatorname{cosec}\dfrac{y}{2}\).

rows.stem: \(\int \dfrac{\cos x}{\sqrt{\sin^2 x + 1}}\, dx\) is equal to :
rows.solution: The numerator is the derivative of \(\sin x\), so substitute \(t = \sin x\), giving \(dt = \cos x\,dx\) and \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2 + 1}}\). This is the standard form \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{t^2 + a^2}} = \log\left|t + \sqrt{t^2 + a^2}\right| + C\) with \(a = 1\). Hence the integral is \(\log\left|t + \sqrt{t^2 + 1}\right| + C\), and restoring \(t = \sin x\) gives \(\log\left|\sin x + \sqrt{1 + \sin^2 x}\right| + C\), which is option (C) \(\log\left|\sin x + \sqrt{1 + \sin^2 x}\right| + C\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Form
rows.stem: If \(x = e^{\sin^{-1} t}\) and \(y = e^{\cos^{-1} t}\), then find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
rows.solution:
Differentiate x and y separately with respect to the parameter t. From \(x = e^{\sin^{-1} t}\), \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\,e^{\sin^{-1} t}\), and from \(y = e^{\cos^{-1} t}\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\,e^{\cos^{-1} t}\). Dividing, the common factor \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}\) cancels and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{e^{\cos^{-1} t}}{e^{\sin^{-1} t}} = -e^{\cos^{-1} t - \sin^{-1} t}\).

At \(t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) both inverse functions equal \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), so the exponent is 0 and \(\left[\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right]_{t = 1/\sqrt{2}} = -e^{0} = -1\). (More generally \(\sin^{-1} t + \cos^{-1} t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -e^{\frac{\pi}{2} - 2\sin^{-1} t}\), which is \(-1\) exactly when \(\sin^{-1} t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).)

rows.stem: Find the sub-interval of \((0, \infty)\) in which \(f(x) = x \log x\) is increasing.
rows.solution: The function \(f(x) = x\log x\) is defined on \((0, \infty)\). By the product rule, \(f'(x) = 1 \cdot \log x + x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} = 1 + \log x\). Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) gives \(\log x = -1\), that is \(x = \dfrac{1}{e}\). Since \(\log x\) is increasing, \(f'(x) = 1 + \log x\) is negative for \(0 < x < \dfrac{1}{e}\) and positive for \(x > \dfrac{1}{e}\). Hence f is increasing on \(\left(\dfrac{1}{e}, \infty\right)\). The interval \(\left[\dfrac{1}{e}, \infty\right)\) may equally be quoted, since \(f'\) vanishes only at the single endpoint \(x = \dfrac{1}{e}\).

Let \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{1 + \sin 2x}\,dx\). Apply the property \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). This sends \(\sin^2 x\) to \(\cos^2 x\), while \(\sin 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \sin(\pi - 2x) = \sin 2x\) leaves the denominator unchanged, so \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{1 + \sin 2x}\,dx\).

Adding the two expressions for I, the numerators add to 1 and \(2I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin 2x}\). Rationalise the integrand by multiplying above and below by \(1 - \sin 2x\): \(\dfrac{1}{1 + \sin 2x} = \dfrac{1 - \sin 2x}{1 - \sin^2 2x} = \dfrac{1 - \sin 2x}{\cos^2 2x} = \sec^2 2x - \sec 2x\tan 2x\).

An antiderivative of this is \(\dfrac{\tan 2x}{2} - \dfrac{\sec 2x}{2} = \dfrac{\sin 2x - 1}{2\cos 2x}\), and multiplying numerator and denominator by \(1 + \sin 2x\) puts it in the equivalent form \(\dfrac{-\cos 2x}{2\left(1 + \sin 2x\right)}\), which is the one to use: it is continuous on the whole of \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), whereas the first form is \(\dfrac{0}{0}\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Evaluating, at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) we get \(\dfrac{-\cos \pi}{2(1 + \sin \pi)} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), and at \(x = 0\) we get \(\dfrac{-1}{2}\). Hence \(2I = \dfrac{1}{2} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 1\), so \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

A note on the middle step: the marking scheme writes this stage as the difference of two separate definite integrals, \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sec^2 2x\,dx - \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sec 2x\tan 2x\,dx\). Taken separately each of those diverges, because \(\cos 2x = 0\) at the interior point \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\); only their difference is finite. The original integrand is perfectly well behaved there, so nothing is wrong with the answer \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) — but the two pieces must be recombined into the single continuous antiderivative above before the limits are put in.

rows.stem: Find the general solution of the differential equation \((x^2 - y^2)\, dx + 2xy\, dy = 0\).
rows.solution:
Write the equation as \(2xy\,dy = -\left(x^2 - y^2\right)dx\), that is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy}\). The right side is unchanged when x and y are both scaled by the same factor, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\), so that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\); the right side becomes \(\dfrac{v^2x^2 - x^2}{2x \cdot vx} = \dfrac{v^2 - 1}{2v}\).

Hence \(v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v^2 - 1}{2v}\), so \(x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v^2 - 1 - 2v^2}{2v} = -\dfrac{1 + v^2}{2v}\). Separating the variables, \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{2v}{1 + v^2}\,dv = -\int \dfrac{dx}{x}\), which integrates to \(\log\left|1 + v^2\right| = -\log|x| + \log|c|\), writing the constant of integration as \(\log|c|\).

Therefore \(1 + v^2 = \dfrac{c}{x}\). Restoring \(v = \dfrac{y}{x}\) gives \(1 + \dfrac{y^2}{x^2} = \dfrac{c}{x}\), and multiplying through by \(x^2\) gives the general solution \(x^2 + y^2 = cx\) — a family of circles through the origin with centres on the x-axis.

As a check, differentiating \(x^2 + y^2 = cx\) gives \(2x + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = c = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{x}\), so \(2x^2 + 2xy\dfrac{dy}{dx} = x^2 + y^2\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy}\), as required.

rows.stem: Solve the differential equation \(\sin x \cos y\, dx + \cos x \sin y\, dy = 0\), given that \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) when \(x = 0\).
rows.solution:
The equation \(\sin x\cos y\,dx + \cos x\sin y\,dy = 0\) separates at once. Dividing throughout by \(\cos x\cos y\) gives \(\tan x\,dx + \tan y\,dy = 0\), that is \(\displaystyle\int \tan y\,dy = -\int \tan x\,dx\).

Since \(\displaystyle\int \tan u\,du = \log|\sec u|\), this gives \(\log|\sec y| = -\log|\sec x| + \log|c|\), so \(\log\left|\sec x\sec y\right| = \log|c|\) and hence \(\sec x\sec y = c\).

Apply the given condition \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) when \(x = 0\): here \(\sec 0 = 1\) and \(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \sqrt{2}\), so \(c = \sqrt{2}\). The particular solution is \(\sec x\sec y = \sqrt{2}\), equivalently \(\cos x\cos y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

As a check, differentiating \(\cos x\cos y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) gives \(-\sin x\cos y\,dx - \cos x\sin y\,dy = 0\), which is exactly the given equation.

rows.stem: Show that a function \(f : R_+ \to A \subset N\), defined as \(f(x) = 4x^2 + 12x + 15\) is one-one. Find set A so that f is onto where \(R_+ = [0, \infty)\). Also, find if there exists \(a \in R_+\) such that \(f(a) = 7\). Justify.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme records that "f defined in the question is not a function", and directs that full marks be awarded to every candidate who attempted it. The reason is the codomain. The domain is stated as \(R_+ = [0, \infty)\), so x ranges over all non-negative REAL numbers, but the codomain is a subset A of the natural numbers N. For a rule to define a function into A, every image must lie in A, and \(4x^2 + 12x + 15\) is not a natural number for most real x — at \(x = 0.1\), for instance, it equals \(16.24\). So no subset A of N can serve as a codomain here, and the map as printed is not a function into N at all. The three things the question asks for are worked out below, reading the codomain as the set of actual images rather than as a subset of N.

One-one. Take \(x_1, x_2 \in R_+\) with \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\), that is \(4x_1^2 + 12x_1 + 15 = 4x_2^2 + 12x_2 + 15\). Cancelling 15 and dividing by 4 gives \(x_1^2 - x_2^2 + 3\left(x_1 - x_2\right) = 0\), which factorises as \(\left(x_1 - x_2\right)\left(x_1 + x_2 + 3\right) = 0\). Since \(x_1, x_2 \ge 0\), the second factor is at least 3 and cannot vanish, so \(x_1 = x_2\) and f is one-one.

The set of images. Completing the square, \(f(x) = 4x^2 + 12x + 15 = (2x + 3)^2 + 6\). As x runs over \([0, \infty)\), \(2x + 3\) runs over \([3, \infty)\), so \((2x + 3)^2\) runs over \([9, \infty)\) and \(f(x)\) runs over \([15, \infty)\). Solving \(y = (2x + 3)^2 + 6\) for x confirms it: \(x = \dfrac{\sqrt{y - 6} - 3}{2}\), which is real and non-negative exactly when \(y \ge 15\). So f is onto if and only if the codomain is taken to be \(A = [15, \infty)\) — and this is precisely where the question breaks down, because that interval is not a subset of N.

Is there \(a \in R_+\) with \(f(a) = 7\)? No. The smallest value f takes on \(R_+\) is \(f(0) = 15\), and \(7 < 15\). Solving directly says the same thing: \(4a^2 + 12a + 15 = 7\) gives \(4a^2 + 12a + 8 = 0\), that is \(a^2 + 3a + 2 = 0\) and \((a + 1)(a + 2) = 0\), whose roots \(a = -1\) and \(a = -2\) both lie outside \(R_+\). So no such a exists.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following Linear Programming Problem graphically :

Maximize \(Z = 8x + 8y\)

subject to the constraints
\(x - 20 \le 0\)
\(2x + 3y \le 120\)
\(2x + y \le 60\)
\(x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0\)
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the corner-point table is headed "Value of Z = 600x + 400y", which is not this paper's objective function; \(600x + 400y\) is the objective of the linear programming question on the sibling paper 65/3/1. Every value tabulated is in fact computed from the objective printed in the question, \(Z = 8x + 8y\) — at \((20, 0)\) it gives 160, not 12000 — so only the column heading is wrong and the answer \(Z_{\max} = 360\) at \((15, 30)\) stands.]

Draw the lines \(x = 20\), \(2x + 3y = 120\) and \(2x + y = 60\) in the first quadrant. Testing the origin satisfies all three inequalities, so the feasible region is the part of the first quadrant lying to the left of \(x = 20\) and below both slant lines. It is a bounded pentagon.

Its corner points come from intersecting the boundary lines in pairs. The origin \(O(0, 0)\) is one. The line \(x = 20\) meets the x-axis at \((20, 0)\), which satisfies both slant constraints. The lines \(x = 20\) and \(2x + y = 60\) meet where \(40 + y = 60\), giving \((20, 20)\); there \(2x + 3y = 40 + 60 = 100 \le 120\), so it is feasible. The lines \(2x + y = 60\) and \(2x + 3y = 120\) meet where subtracting gives \(2y = 60\), so \(y = 30\) and then \(2x = 30\), giving \((15, 30)\); there \(x = 15 \le 20\), so it is feasible. Finally \(2x + 3y = 120\) meets the y-axis at \((0, 40)\), where \(2x + y = 40 \le 60\). So the corners are \((0, 0)\), \((20, 0)\), \((20, 20)\), \((15, 30)\) and \((0, 40)\).

Now evaluate \(Z = 8x + 8y = 8(x + y)\) at each. At \((0, 0)\), \(Z = 0\); at \((20, 0)\), \(Z = 160\); at \((20, 20)\), \(Z = 320\); at \((15, 30)\), \(Z = 360\); at \((0, 40)\), \(Z = 320\).

The feasible region is bounded, so Z attains its maximum at a corner point. Hence \(Z_{\max} = 360\), attained at the point \((15, 30)\). (Since Z is a multiple of \(x + y\), this is just the feasible point that maximises \(x + y\), namely \(15 + 30 = 45\).)
